missing_spec_content.spec_text: A vector quantity may be represented by an arrow. The length of the arrow represents the magnitude, and the direction of the arrow the direction of the vector quantity.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson never explains that vectors can be shown as arrows, or that arrow length shows magnitude and arrow direction shows direction.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: The speed of a moving object is rarely constant. When people walk, run or travel in a car their speed is constantly changing.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson does not teach that real speeds are rarely constant.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: The speed at which a person can walk, run or cycle depends on many factors including: age, terrain, fitness and distance travelled.
missing_spec_content.why: The factors that affect a person's speed are not mentioned.
The typical running speed is missing. The lesson lists walking, cycling, car, sound and light, but not running, which the spec requires students to recall.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: as well as the typical values of speed for different types of transportation systems.
missing_spec_content.why: Only one transport value is given ('car on a motorway ≈ 30 m/s'). Other transport systems (for example trains or planes) are not covered.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: It is not only moving objects that have varying speed. The speed of sound and the speed of the wind also vary.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson does not say that the speed of sound and wind speed vary.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: A typical value for the speed of sound in air is 330 m/s.
missing_spec_content.why: The spec's typical value (330 m/s) is not taught. The lesson gives 'speed of sound in air ≈ 340 m/s' (keyPoints[1].content, keyPoints[1].writeBullets[5], revisionCardBullets[11]). That is physically reasonable, but it is not the value the spec states.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Students should be able to make measurements of distance and time and then calculate speeds of objects.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson does not cover how to measure distance and time practically to find a speed.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: (HT only) Students should be able to explain qualitatively, with examples, that motion in a circle involves constant speed but changing velocity.
missing_spec_content.why: Circular motion at constant speed but changing velocity is not taught.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: (HT only) If an object is accelerating, its speed at any particular time can be determined by drawing a tangent and measuring the gradient of the distance–time graph at that time.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson says a curved d-t line means changing speed, but never teaches drawing a tangent to find the speed at a particular time.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Students should be able to draw distance–time graphs from measurements and extract and interpret lines and slopes of distance–time graphs, translating information between graphical and numerical form.
missing_spec_content.why: Drawing d-t graphs from measured data is not covered. Only interpreting graph shapes is taught.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Students should be able to estimate the magnitude of everyday accelerations.
missing_spec_content.why: No typical everyday acceleration values are given, and the lesson does not show how to estimate them.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: draw velocity–time graphs from measurements and interpret lines and slopes to determine acceleration
missing_spec_content.why: Drawing v-t graphs from measured data is not covered.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: (HT only) measure, when appropriate, the area under a velocity–time graph by counting squares.
missing_spec_content.why: Counting squares to find the area under a v-t graph is not taught. Only the triangle and trapezium formulas are given.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: An object falling through a fluid initially accelerates due to the force of gravity. Eventually the resultant force will be zero and the object will move at its terminal velocity.
missing_spec_content.why: Terminal velocity is taught only for falling through air. The general idea of falling through any fluid (for example a liquid) is not mentioned.

above_gcse.why: This equation is not in the specification. The spec only requires a = Δv/t and v² − u² = 2as for uniform acceleration. Teaching extra 'SUVAT' equations could confuse students about which equations they must know.
The spec does not use the term 'SUVAT' or present a set of equations of motion. The 'three values, find a fourth' framework goes beyond the spec.
s = ½at² is not in the specification and is not taught anywhere in the lesson.

above_gcse.text: Equations of motion questions nearly always give you three values and ask for a fourth. Find your u, v, a, s and t before writing anything.
above_gcse.why: This assumes a SUVAT-style problem framework that the spec does not require.

factual_errors.correction: For 300 m east then 400 m north, the displacement is 500 m at about 53° north of east (a bearing of about 037°). This is not north-east, which would be 45°. The spec says students must 'express a displacement in terms of both the magnitude and direction', so the direction should be stated precisely.

wrong_terms.text: Equation: v = d/t. Rearrangements: d = vt, t = d/v.
wrong_terms.spec_term: s = v t (distance travelled = speed × time), with distance given the symbol s
distance, s, in metres, m (the spec defines s in v² − u² = 2as as distance)

wrong_terms.text: The net force and the acceleration both decrease.
Parachute opens. Drag increases hugely, so the net force is now upward.
Terminal velocity: air resistance = weight → zero net force → constant velocity
Parachute opens → massive drag → decelerates to new lower terminal velocity

checkpoint_mismatch.why: This assumes checkpoint '1' sits with the first key point. It asks for a speed calculation ('A car travels 240m in 8s...'), which is taught in keyPoints[1]. It does not test the scalar/vector distinction.
This assumes checkpoint '2' sits with the second key point. It asks what the gradient of a velocity-time graph shows, which is taught in keyPoints[2], not in the distance-time key point.

The correctFeedback uses 's = ½at²', which no key point teaches. The answer 44.1 m is correct and can be reached with the taught equations (v = u + at, then s = ½(u + v)t), as the wrongFeedback shows. However, the main feedback relies on an untaught equation.

not_checked: The lesson does not say which key point each checkpoint sits with. The mismatches above assume checkpoint N follows keyPoints[N-1]. There are 4 checkpoints and 5 key points, so keyPoints[4] (terminal velocity) has no checkpoint under that assumption.

Claims about exam frequency and mark values (for example 'Area under v-t graph calculations come up as 6-mark questions', 'Gradient calculations on d-t graphs come up almost every year', 'v² = u² + 2as is the most tested', 'a very common 4-mark question') cannot be checked against the specification text.
